Lab 3: Supervised Learning (Regression)¶

Name: Carlos Gutierrez
Student ID: 9118309
Section: 1

This notebook has two parts:

  • Part A: detect fraudulent credit card transactions with logistic regression.
  • Part B: predict insurance costs with linear regression.

In both parts the data is split 70% for training and 30% for testing.

Data sources (files go in the data/ folder, which is not tracked in git):

  • Credit card fraud: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mlg-ulb/creditcardfraud (data/creditcard.csv)
  • Insurance: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mirichoi0218/insurance (data/insurance.csv)

Setup¶

In [1]:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import (accuracy_score, confusion_matrix, classification_report,
                             precision_score, recall_score, f1_score, roc_auc_score,
                             roc_curve, precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score,
                             r2_score, mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error)

RANDOM_STATE = 42
TEST_SIZE = 0.3
CARD_PATH = "data/creditcard.csv"
INSURANCE_PATH = "data/insurance.csv"

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", 50)
pd.set_option("display.width", 150)

Part A: Credit Card Fraud Detection (Logistic Regression)¶

Goal: build a model that decides whether a credit card transaction is fraudulent (Class = 1) or genuine (Class = 0).

A5. Preprocessing¶

  • Separate the features (X) from the target (y).
  • V1 to V28 are already on a similar scale, but Time and Amount are not, so they will be standardised.
  • The split is done first and the scaler is fitted on the training data only, so no information from the test set leaks into training.
In [12]:
X = card.drop(columns="Class")
y = card["Class"]
print(X.shape, y.shape)

(283726, 30) (283726,)

A6. Train / test split (70% / 30%)¶

The split is stratified so both sets keep the same small fraction of fraud cases.

A7. Build the logistic regression model¶

In [15]:
log_reg = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
log_reg.fit(X_train_s, y_train)
print("Model trained.")

Model trained.

A8. Evaluation¶

The required metric is accuracy. Because of the class imbalance I also report the confusion matrix, precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC.

In [16]:
def evaluate(model, X_tr, y_tr, X_te, y_te, name):
    pred_tr, pred_te = model.predict(X_tr), model.predict(X_te)
    proba_te = model.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1]
    print(f"--- {name} ---")
    print("Train accuracy: %.5f" % accuracy_score(y_tr, pred_tr))
    print("Test accuracy:  %.5f" % accuracy_score(y_te, pred_te))
    print("Test precision: %.4f" % precision_score(y_te, pred_te))
    print("Test recall:    %.4f" % recall_score(y_te, pred_te))
    print("Test F1:        %.4f" % f1_score(y_te, pred_te))
    print("Test ROC-AUC:   %.4f" % roc_auc_score(y_te, proba_te))
    print()
    print(classification_report(y_te, pred_te, target_names=["genuine", "fraud"], digits=4))
    return pred_te, proba_te

pred_base, proba_base = evaluate(log_reg, X_train_s, y_train, X_test_s, y_test, "Logistic regression (baseline)")

In [17]:
def plot_cm(y_true, y_pred, title):
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt="d", cmap="Blues",
                xticklabels=["genuine", "fraud"], yticklabels=["genuine", "fraud"])
    plt.xlabel("Predicted"); plt.ylabel("Actual"); plt.title(title)
    plt.show()

plot_cm(y_test, pred_base, "Confusion matrix (baseline)")
In [18]:
fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, proba_base)
prec, rec, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_test, proba_base)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5))
axes[0].plot(fpr, tpr, label="AUC = %.4f" % roc_auc_score(y_test, proba_base))
axes[0].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--")
axes[0].set_xlabel("False positive rate"); axes[0].set_ylabel("True positive rate")
axes[0].set_title("ROC curve"); axes[0].legend()

axes[1].plot(rec, prec, label="AP = %.4f" % average_precision_score(y_test, proba_base))
axes[1].set_xlabel("Recall"); axes[1].set_ylabel("Precision")
axes[1].set_title("Precision-recall curve"); axes[1].legend()
plt.show()

Reading the results: accuracy is very high, but that is mostly because genuine transactions are almost all of the data. Recall (how many frauds are caught) is the number that tells how useful the model really is.

A9. Extras: handling the class imbalance¶

Class weights¶

Giving the rare class more weight makes the model pay more attention to fraud cases.

In [19]:
log_reg_bal = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
log_reg_bal.fit(X_train_s, y_train)
pred_bal, proba_bal = evaluate(log_reg_bal, X_train_s, y_train, X_test_s, y_test, "Logistic regression (balanced weights)")
plot_cm(y_test, pred_bal, "Confusion matrix (balanced weights)")

Decision threshold tuning¶

By default a transaction is flagged as fraud when the probability is above 0.5. I pick a better threshold using a validation set taken from the training data (so the test set stays untouched), choosing the value with the best F1.

In [20]:
X_fit, X_val, y_fit, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_train_s, y_train, test_size=0.2, stratify=y_train, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)

model_val = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced", random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
model_val.fit(X_fit, y_fit)

p, r, thr = precision_recall_curve(y_val, model_val.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1])
f1s = 2 * p[:-1] * r[:-1] / (p[:-1] + r[:-1] + 1e-12)
best_thr = thr[np.argmax(f1s)]
print("Best threshold on validation data: %.6f (F1 = %.4f)" % (best_thr, f1s.max()))
print("The balanced model pushes its probabilities towards 0 or 1, so the best cut-off ends up very close to 1.")

plt.plot(thr, p[:-1], label="precision")
plt.plot(thr, r[:-1], label="recall")
plt.plot(thr, f1s, label="F1")
plt.axvline(best_thr, color="k", linestyle="--")
plt.xlabel("Threshold"); plt.legend(); plt.title("Validation metrics by threshold")
plt.show()

Best threshold on validation data: 1.000000 (F1 = 0.7869)
The balanced model pushes its probabilities towards 0 or 1, so the best cut-off ends up very close to 1.
In [21]:
pred_thr = (log_reg_bal.predict_proba(X_test_s)[:, 1] >= best_thr).astype(int)
print("Test accuracy: %.5f" % accuracy_score(y_test, pred_thr))
print(classification_report(y_test, pred_thr, target_names=["genuine", "fraud"], digits=4))
plot_cm(y_test, pred_thr, "Confusion matrix (balanced weights + tuned threshold)")

A10. Part A summary¶

In [23]:
final_acc = accuracy_score(y_test, pred_base)
print("Required model (baseline logistic regression) test accuracy: %.4f%%" % (final_acc * 100))

Required model (baseline logistic regression) test accuracy: 99.9107%
  • The baseline logistic regression reaches a very high accuracy, as required, but accuracy is inflated by the imbalance.
  • Class weights raise recall (about 89% of frauds caught instead of about 57%), but precision falls to about 5% and accuracy drops to about 97%, because many genuine transactions get flagged.
  • Tuning the threshold keeps accuracy high and gives the best balance of precision and recall (F1 about 0.80 against 0.68 for the baseline).
  • Limitation: a linear model on anonymised features is a simple approach. Real systems would try other models and use cost-based evaluation.

B4. Preprocessing¶

  • sex and smoker have two values, so they become 0/1.
  • region has four values, so it is one-hot encoded (one column dropped to avoid redundant columns).
  • Linear regression does not need scaled features to work, so I leave the numbers in their original units. That also keeps the coefficients easy to read.
In [33]:
data = ins.copy()
data["sex"] = data["sex"].map({"female": 0, "male": 1})
data["smoker"] = data["smoker"].map({"no": 0, "yes": 1})
data = pd.get_dummies(data, columns=["region"], drop_first=True, dtype=int)

B7. Evaluation¶

In [37]:
def reg_metrics(model, X_tr, y_tr, X_te, y_te):
    out = {}
    for label, Xs, ys in [("train", X_tr, y_tr), ("test", X_te, y_te)]:
        pred = model.predict(Xs)
        out[label] = {"R2": r2_score(ys, pred),
                      "MAE": mean_absolute_error(ys, pred),
                      "MSE": mean_squared_error(ys, pred),
                      "RMSE": np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(ys, pred))}
    return pd.DataFrame(out).round(4)

metrics_base = reg_metrics(lin_reg, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test)

Reading the results: the test R² shows how much of the variation in charges the model explains. The residual plot has a pattern (errors are larger and uneven for expensive cases), which says a straight line misses some structure, mainly the combined effect of smoking and BMI. The next section tries to capture that.

B8. Extras: feature engineering¶

Ideas based on the plots above:

  • age_squared: cost grows faster at higher ages.
  • obese: BMI of 30 or more.
  • smoker_bmi: interaction of smoking and BMI (the scatter plot showed smokers with high BMI cost much more).
  • Log-transforming charges to reduce its skew (predictions are converted back to dollars for evaluation).
In [39]:
def add_features(df):
    out = df.copy()
    out["age_squared"] = out["age"] ** 2
    out["obese"] = (out["bmi"] >= 30).astype(int)
    out["smoker_bmi"] = out["smoker"] * out["bmi"]
    out["smoker_obese"] = out["smoker"] * out["obese"]
    return out

X_train_fe, X_test_fe = add_features(X_train), add_features(X_test)

# Model 2: engineered features, charges in dollars
lin_fe = LinearRegression().fit(X_train_fe, y_train)
pred_fe = lin_fe.predict(X_test_fe)

# Model 3: engineered features, log of charges
lin_log = LinearRegression().fit(X_train_fe, np.log(y_train))
pred_log = np.exp(lin_log.predict(X_test_fe))

rows = []
for name, pred in [("Baseline", pred_test),
                   ("Engineered features", pred_fe),
                   ("Engineered + log(charges)", pred_log)]:
    rows.append({"model": name,
                 "R2": r2_score(y_test, pred),
                 "MAE": mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred),
                 "RMSE": np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, pred))})
comparison_b = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("model").round(4)
comparison_b

The interaction terms help because smokers and non-smokers follow different cost patterns. The log version is shown for comparison and it does worse: after converting the predictions back to dollars the errors on expensive cases become large, so it is not used. Its metrics are measured in dollars, so the numbers are comparable.

B9. Prediction system¶

A function that takes the details of a new person and returns the predicted yearly insurance cost. It uses the baseline model (the one required by the lab) and the improved model.

In [41]:
def predict_cost(age, sex, bmi, children, smoker, region):
    row = pd.DataFrame([{
        "age": age,
        "sex": 1 if sex.lower() == "male" else 0,
        "bmi": bmi,
        "children": children,
        "smoker": 1 if smoker.lower() == "yes" else 0,
        "region_northwest": int(region.lower() == "northwest"),
        "region_southeast": int(region.lower() == "southeast"),
        "region_southwest": int(region.lower() == "southwest"),
    }])[X.columns]
    base = lin_reg.predict(row)[0]
    improved = lin_fe.predict(add_features(row))[0]
    return base, improved

examples = [
    dict(age=31, sex="female", bmi=25.7, children=0, smoker="no", region="southeast"),
    dict(age=45, sex="male", bmi=33.5, children=2, smoker="yes", region="northeast"),
    dict(age=22, sex="male", bmi=22.0, children=0, smoker="no", region="southwest"),
]
for e in examples:
    b, i = predict_cost(**e)
    print(e)
    print("  Baseline model:  $%.2f" % b)
    print("  Improved model:  $%.2f\n" % i)

B10. Part B summary¶

In [42]:
print("Required model (baseline linear regression) test R2: %.4f" % metrics_base.loc["R2", "test"])
print("Test MAE: $%.2f, Test RMSE: $%.2f" % (metrics_base.loc["MAE", "test"], metrics_base.loc["RMSE", "test"]))

Required model (baseline linear regression) test R2: 0.7724
Test MAE: $4181.82, Test RMSE: $6240.21
  • Smoking status is the strongest driver of cost, followed by age and BMI.
  • The baseline linear regression explains most of the variation in charges, with typical errors of a few thousand dollars.
  • Adding interaction and non-linear terms improves R² (about 0.77 to 0.88) and lowers the error. The plain model can predict very low costs for some young non-smokers, which the extra features partly fix.
  • Limitation: the dataset is small (about 1,300 rows), so results on new data could vary.

Conclusions¶

  • Part A is a classification problem. Accuracy looked excellent but hid how few frauds the baseline model catches, so precision, recall and F1 were needed. Class weights and threshold tuning showed the trade-off between catching fraud and raising false alarms.
  • Part B is a regression problem measured with R², MAE and RMSE. Encoding categorical columns and adding features that capture combined effects gave a better fit than the plain model.
  • In both parts the split was done before any fitting (and scaling) to avoid leaking information from the test set.
